p: Elena gave Priya the Copilot rollout and a quarter to get every engineer on it.
Priya chose Copilot Business, moved the people on personal plans onto company seats, and turned it on in waves, so Ken could fence off the patient adjacent code first.
Anders asked Copilot to explain a module he wrote, caught it getting one thing backwards, and called it a decent junior he has to check.
Elena wanted a target for each engineer's acceptance rate. Priya talked her into measuring team results instead.
Then, at 2:14 on Sunday night, Tomasz wrote from Kraków. His team had assigned an issue to Copilot, waited in their editors, and nothing happened.
Tomasz Nowak. Runs engineering in Kraków. His people sign up first for everything new.
Anders Lindqvist. Priya's old mentor, now trying Copilot on his own Terraform.
Devin Marsh. Engineer. Always looking for the setting that makes it faster.
Renata Vega. Junior engineer, a few weeks in. She asks what everyone else won't.
Ken Ito. Security lead. His exclusions keep Copilot out of patient adjacent code.
Joyce Cho. The CTO, and the rollout's sponsor. She likes a chart.
Chapter two. Two Kinds of Agent.

She didn't sleep after that. At 2:40 she gave up, made tea, and sat at the kitchen table with her laptop and the GitHub docs, reading the way she used to read for exams, with a pen in her hand even though there was nothing to write on.

By five she had the answer, and it was embarrassing in the useful way. Copilot had two things that people called an agent. One lived inside your editor and worked while you watched. The other lived on GitHub, and once you handed it an issue it went off and did the work somewhere else, on its own, and came back with a pull request. Kraków had used the second one and waited for the first.

She typed a reply to Tomasz and deleted it, because a paragraph at five in the morning wasn't going to fix it. Can I join your 3 PM? I'll show you where it went. I didn't know either until an hour ago.
His answer came back in under a minute. Kraków was eight hours ahead, and he'd been at his desk since nine their time. Yes. Bring coffee for yourself. We already had ours.

At 6:30 her phone buzzed with five new photos of index cards, purple felt tip on lined white. Asha had been up too. Thirty years of nights did that to a person, and retirement hadn't undone it. Across the top card she'd written: Week three. You don't need to know everything. You need to know who's on your shift.
Under it, smaller, a second line. And who's on the next one.
Asha's first card was about staffing. Some help works beside you. Some help works the next shift while you sleep. Don't confuse them, and don't manage them the same way.
The second card was the one Priya taped to her monitor. Night shift hands off. Day shift takes report and checks the patient. Nobody takes report and goes home.

The third card was the only one in Asha's handwriting that looked rushed, as if she'd written it fast so she couldn't talk herself out of it. My first year. I was twenty nine, and the off going nurse was someone I wanted to be. She said the count was right, and I signed without counting. It was off by one vial. Three of us spent until four in the morning finding it in the wrong drawer. A signature means you checked. That's all it means.
The fourth card was a list. Small job, small team. Long shift, clean handoff. Send a runner instead of leaving the bedside.
The last card had a door drawn on it. Every new tool on the cart is a new way in. Know who brought it and what it can reach.

At seven she was on video with Kraków, a cup of coffee she didn't want in her hand. Tomasz sat at the head of a table with four of his engineers. Behind them the window was full of a gray October afternoon.
We assigned the logging issue to Copilot at ten this morning. Then we opened our editors and waited for it to start. Nothing happened. So, is it broken, or are we?
Nobody at the table was smiling. They had been the first team to sign up for anything new for two years, and Priya could see they were bracing to be the team that got it wrong.

She shares her screen and opens the issue. Copilot had reacted to the assignment at 10:01 their time and linked a draft pull request a minute later. It had worked for about forty minutes in its own environment, pushing commits, and just before eleven it had asked Tomasz for a review. Everybody had been watching their editors. Tomasz laughs once, short. So it finished before lunch, and we kept it waiting all afternoon.

The coding agent works on GitHub, asynchronously, in an environment GitHub Actions provides, and reports back through a draft pull request. Agent mode is the one that works in your editor while you watch. To follow the coding agent, look at the issue, the pull request, and its session log.
The pull request changed nine files. It had a tidy summary, a link that said View session, and a yellow banner Priya hadn't seen before: workflows awaiting approval.
Tomasz clicked Approve. GitHub didn't let him.
I assigned it. I'm the one who knows what I wanted. Why can't I approve it?

The person who assigned the agent can't approve its pull request, so Priya asks for a second reviewer. The newest engineer on Tomasz's team takes it, a little surprised to be picked. She reads the diff and finds that the new logging writes the full request body, which in staging includes test patient identifiers. She leaves a comment on the pull request: "@copilot, log the request ID only, never the body." Twenty minutes later there's a new commit. The workflows run once someone approves them, and they pass. Tomasz watches the whole thing, then leans back and takes his glasses off.

GitHub builds independent review into the coding agent. The developer who asked for the work can't approve it, the agent can't approve or merge its own pull request, and by default workflows wait for someone with write access to approve them. You ask for changes by mentioning @copilot in a comment.
Tuesday at 11:20 the staging database came back empty. Two days of test data that Kraków had seeded for their integration tests were gone.

It took Priya fifteen minutes to read the session. Anders had been in agent mode, asking it to fix drift in the staging Terraform. It proposed running terraform apply with the flag that skips its own yes or no question. Anders had clicked Continue while he was on another call. If he'd run a plan first, it would have told him the database was about to be replaced.
Anders had been using agent mode for a week without telling anyone, which was its own kind of news.

She looked at her old runbook on the desk, the one with "ask Anders" in the margins in her own handwriting. Asha's rushed card was still on her phone, three photos in, the one about the narcotic count she signed at twenty nine without counting. A signature means you checked. She texted Asha before she could stop herself.
A text from Asha. Who knows he didn't read it? Him, or just you?

She finds him in the small room by the kitchen, laptop closed. She brings the runbook and doesn't open it. Half the pages in here say ask Anders, she says. So I'm asking. What happened? He turns his closed laptop a quarter turn on the table, then back. I told sixty people I'd be on call for this. I didn't think I'd be the page. It looked like something I'd type. That's the whole problem. It looked like me. They write the note together. Agent mode never runs a state changing infrastructure command without a reviewed plan, and nobody approves a command they haven't read. Anders posts it under his own name. Tomasz replies first. Thank you for saying it was you.

An approval only counts if someone reads what they're approving. Validating AI output includes the commands it proposes, not only the code. Going to the person first and then fixing the process keeps a mistake useful instead of shameful.
By Tuesday afternoon everyone had heard about staging. Devin had a different conclusion than everyone else.
Hot take. Clicking Continue fifty times a day is what made him stop reading. There's a setting that approves terminal commands automatically. Turn it on and I ship twice as fast.
He wasn't entirely wrong about the first part. Priya had seen the setting.

She and Devin write the list together: run the tests, run the linter, list files, show git status. Everything else still asks. Devin grumbles that it's only half of what he wanted. A week later he admits the prompts he still gets are the ones he'd want to read anyway.

Agent mode asks before running commands that aren't auto approved, and you can approve once, for the session or workspace, or by rule. VS Code already auto approves common read only commands. A narrow, shared allow list for harmless commands cuts the noise that makes people stop reading. Anything that changes state keeps a human approval.
Wednesday morning Renata came to Priya's desk instead of messaging. She'd been thinking about it for a while.

I have to rename a field across the API, the model, and two tests. Four files. I know exactly which ones. Everyone says use agent mode for everything now. Is that what I should do? It feels like a lot for four files.

She opens Copilot Edits, adds the four files herself, and describes the rename. Copilot proposes a change in each one. She keeps three and stops on the fourth, where it renamed a JSON key the hospital interface reads. Is that one supposed to change? It wasn't. She undoes it, and learns more about Lumen's contract with its customers in five minutes than in a month of reading.

Copilot Edits makes changes across several files from one conversation. When you pick the files, Copilot only proposes changes there, and you review each one before you keep it. Agent mode is for when you need Copilot to find the files itself.
Wednesday afternoon, Tomasz again, on a call with his camera off.

We started an agent session this morning to refactor the scheduler. At ten it was brilliant. We agreed at the start to keep the old retry behavior. Now it keeps suggesting we remove it, and it brings back ideas we said no to two hours ago. It's like talking to someone who's been in the same meeting since breakfast.
Priya thought of Asha's fourth card. Long shift, clean handoff.

Tomasz writes five lines: what the refactor is for, the retry rule, two ideas already rejected, and the files involved. The new session starts clean. When it needs to read four hundred lines of old scheduler logs, it hands that to a subagent and gets back three sentences. A fresh session and five lines. Of course.

Every session has a limited context window, and the chat history is part of what fills it. Start a new session per task with a short summary of what still matters. A subagent does a focused job in its own context and returns only the result.
Ken caught her at the end of Wednesday, at her desk, standing, which meant it wouldn't take long and it mattered.
The Lumen repositories are behind content exclusions. If someone assigns the coding agent an issue in one of them, or opens one in agent mode, do my exclusions hold?
Nora was copied on his calendar invite for Thursday, so whatever Priya said would end up in the evidence log.

They read the limitations together. When they checked, the docs said agent mode in VS Code didn't honor exclusions at all, and the coding agent's support was still a public preview. Ken is quiet for a second. So my fence has a gate in it. They take the Lumen repositories off the coding agent's list, and Ken adds a line to the guide: no agent mode in excluded repositories until the docs say otherwise. Nora logs it with the date.

Content exclusions have documented limits, and the list changes. Before you count on one, read the current limitations, and close the gap with another control, like keeping the coding agent off those repositories.
Thursday Anders came to her with something he'd found, and it was the first time all week he'd sounded like himself.

There's an MCP server on GitHub that connects agent mode to Postgres and to our ticket tracker. The agent could read the staging schema itself, look up the ticket, and stop guessing. I'll set it up for infra with my credentials this afternoon.
His credentials were the admin ones. Priya thought about Tuesday, and then about how to say that to him.

She asks him to read the server's code first. It's two hundred lines. I can read two hundred lines. He finds it sends every query to an analytics service run by someone none of them have heard of. They use the GitHub MCP server for tickets and a small server they write themselves against a read only database user. Priya checks the organization's MCP policy before anyone turns it on. Anders says it out loud: I'm reading everything this week.

MCP is an open standard that connects agents to outside tools and data. Each server is a new way in. Use servers you trust, give them the narrowest access that works, and follow the organization's policy on MCP.
Kraków had gone from wary to hungry in three days. Thursday evening Tomasz sent her a link to a new issue.
Issue 412. The title says migrate the auth service to the new identity provider. The description, all of it: move the auth service to the new identity provider. Should be straightforward.
It was assigned to Copilot. The auth service touched every login at every hospital that licensed Lumen.

Tomasz and two of his engineers spend an hour on the design. Then they write six small issues, each with a clear goal, acceptance criteria, and the files involved. The agent gets the four that are routine. People keep the two that decide how logins work.

The coding agent does best on well scoped issues with clear descriptions and acceptance criteria. Keep design decisions and the most sensitive work with people, and hand the agent the parts you can describe completely.
Friday morning Joyce stopped by with a chart. The coding agent's pull requests from Kraków were piling up in review.
Review is the slow part now. If the checks are green, can we just auto merge the agent's pull requests? It wrote the tests too.

Joyce wants something for the chart, so Priya gives her the real bottleneck: the issues were too big to review quickly. Smaller issues make smaller pull requests. By the next Friday review time is down by half, with a person on every one.
The coding agent can't approve or merge its own pull request, and its work gets reviewed like anyone's. Speed up review by scoping smaller issues, not by removing the reviewer.

Priya had thirty minutes at the Friday engineering sync. It had been a long week of the same confusion in different clothes. Kraków had waited in their editors for an agent that lived on GitHub. Someone had asked whether agent mode opens pull requests. Devin thought Copilot CLI was just chat in a terminal window.
Anders, in the front row again, had his arms folded. It looked different this week.

She does the inline and chat parts herself. Then she hands agent mode to Anders, who reads every command out loud before he approves it, and the coding agent to Tomasz, whose team knows it best now. Renata asks the question everyone was thinking: So agent mode never opens a pull request by itself? Tomasz answers before Priya can. Not by itself. Agent mode works in your editor while you watch. The one on GitHub is the one that opens the pull request.

Each surface has its own job. Inline suggestions help as you type, chat answers and explains, agent mode makes multi file changes in the editor while you approve, the coding agent works on GitHub and opens a pull request, and the CLI works in the terminal. Seeing them side by side clears up the confusion.

By Friday evening there was a whiteboard in the big room with two columns on it in somebody's square handwriting. Agent mode: in your editor, you watch, you approve. Coding agent: on GitHub, it works while you don't, you take report. Somebody had drawn a small coffee cup at the bottom of the second column.
At 5:30 Anders requested her review on a pull request, the staging Terraform fix.
The description had three lines. Copilot wrote most of this. I read every line. Read it again anyway.

She read every line. It was good. She left one comment, on a variable called db that really meant the staging database, so he'd know she'd gone through all of it, and hit Approve. Six months ago every pull request she opened had his name in the reviewer box. She sat for a minute looking at hers in his.

On the way out she saw Devin's pull request in the feed, a cleanup of the discharge window code. Opened at 5:41, approved at 5:49, merged at 5:52. She wrote his name at the top of Monday's list and went home.

Saturday she drove out to Aurora. The garage door was up and her father was at the lathe he'd bought used when the shop closed, turning a bushing for the neighbor's mower. Asha sat on an upturned paint bucket with a paper plate of samosas. She never needed much of a reason.
This agent, he said, not looking up from the cut. Works while you sleep?
Some of it. Then somebody reads every line in the morning.
Huh. The chuck wound down. So it's a second shift.
You never answered my text, Asha said.
He knew. He was sitting in the little room with his laptop shut. Asha nodded slowly. Then you didn't have to tell him anything. You just had to go in.
Her father wiped his hands and gave her the setup sheet and the micrometer, same as when she was nine and stood on a milk crate to see. Read me the numbers before I cut.
She read them. Bore, outside diameter, length, each one to the thousandth. Again, he said. She read them again, slower, and he nodded and reached for the switch.
